title: SYSK Selects: How HeLa Cells Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun (picked by Josh) of the episode on HeLa cells. Covers Henrietta Lacks, a Baltimore woman whose cervical cancer cells, taken without her knowledge at Johns Hopkins in the 1950s, became the first immortal human cell line, grown by Dr. Gey's tissue culture lab. Discusses HPV integration and the Mic gene theory for their immortality, apoptosis and the Hayflick limit, the cells' use in polio, HPV, and other research, contamination of other cell lines, the family's unconsented discovery and misleading blood-test call, the 1990 Moore v. Regents case, Rebecca Skloot's book The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks, and the 2013 HeLa genome access arrangement with family representation. Closes with a listener mail about a homebrew biodiesel setup and an outro.

segments.title: Rerun intro and Josh's pick
segments.summary: Chuck introduces this Saturday Selects episode, which Josh picked. Josh explains the appeal of mixing history and science and notes the listener requests about the pronunciation of HeLa and the Lacks name.

segments.title: Henrietta Lacks and the first immortal cells
segments.summary: Henrietta Lacks, a Black woman in Baltimore, had cervical cancer after giving birth to her fifth child. Because Johns Hopkins was the only local place treating African Americans, she was treated there. Dr. Gey's tissue culture lab grew cells from her tumor, which kept dividing and doubling every 24 hours, the first immortal human line. She died October 4, 1951, and the hosts describe the painful, primitive treatment she received.

segments.title: Naming the cells and buying HeLa cells today
segments.summary: The cells were named after Henrietta Lacks, with a long-standing misidentification as Helen Lane or Helen Larson. Consent was not required at the time, and Gey gave cells away free. Today HeLa cell lines are sold commercially, with prices ranging from about $250 to thousands of dollars, with nonprofit discounts.

segments.title: Why HeLa cells are immortal: HPV and the MYC gene
segments.summary: The hosts explain the leading theory, reported in Nature, that HPV inserted its genetic material near the MYC regulatory gene in Lacks's DNA, possibly driving rapid division. They note it is only a theory and that Rebecca Skloot accepts it. Josh says this was not known during the book tour.

segments.title: Apoptosis, the Hayflick limit, and cancer
segments.summary: Apoptosis is programmed cell death, a normal process that balances cell division and removes unneeded cells, including webbing between developing fingers. Normal cells divide roughly 40 to 60 times before dying, known as the Hayflick limit. Cancer cells evade this limit, and HeLa cells are extremely hardy, airborne, and contaminated other cell lines by the early 1970s.

segments.title: Family discovery, deception, and the research legacy
segments.summary: In the early 1970s researchers contacted the Lacks family to get their DNA for identifying HeLa contamination. The family was confused, and the call was misleading because it suggested the children might have cancer. Johns Hopkins never called back. HeLa cells contributed to research on polio (Salk vaccine testing), HPV vaccine development, measles, mumps, tuberculosis, HIV, and Parkinson's, and to standardized cell culture and shipping, with more than 11,000 patents mentioned.

segments.title: Legal rights, the HeLa genome, and the family's recognition
segments.summary: The family found the cell line was a large industry without compensation. Courts ruled that tissue removed from the body does not belong to the donor, citing a 1990 case involving a leukemia patient's cells. In 2013 the NIH gave two descendants a seat on the HeLa Genome Data Access Working Group after a European agency published the HeLa genome. The family received an apology and scholarships, and the hosts note a Henrietta Lacks Foundation.

segments.title: Listener mail: homebrew biodiesel
segments.summary: Ben writes about his father's homebrew biodiesel setup in a garage, which produces 90-gallon batches from used vegetable oil and fuels family vehicles and a boat.

segments.title: Sign-off and further reading
segments.summary: The hosts recommend Rebecca Skloot's The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks and invite listeners to contact the show and visit the website.
